entry.title: Fun With GTFS
entry.summary: For about six months back in 2022, GTFS was my obsession. The General Transit Feed Specification (or GTFS) is one of the many…
entry.content:
For about six months back in 2022, GTFS was my obsession. The General Transit Feed Specification (or GTFS) is one of the many unsung heroes of city life in the 21st Century. GTFS is a common data standard used by public transportation systems across the globe. It means that if a software application wants to work with transit data, it simply needs to decode the standard file structure outlined by GTFS. 

For someone interested in transportation, GTFS provides a treasure trove of opportunities. If I want to know where each bus stop is in Nairobi, Kenya --- it's easily available. If I want to explore the timetables for the metro system of Fortaleza, Brazil --- they've got that too.

When I worked for the regional planning agency serving the Louisville metropolitan area, I was approached by one of the planners for assistance in conducting a study of the efficacy of using Louisville's public transportation to commute to work. It was an interesting prospect and was similar to a study he had organized in New Orleans, which in turn was based off a study done by the University of Minnesota. 

GTFS turned out to be a key component in performing the spatial / temporal analysis required to conduct our study. I ended up communicating  with a developer at ESRI (not the last time I'd be doing that) where I helped identify a bug with their GTFS analysis toolbox, which was then resolved. 

Rather than explain the entire process in this blog post, I invite you to take a look at the Story Map I created to present our findings. I used this as a visual aid when I spoke about this project at both the 2022 Kentucky Association of Mapping Professionals conference and 2022 Indiana Association of MPOs conference. 

While I was crafting my presentation I stumbled upon an old write-up online detailing how to create neat visualizations of GTFS data, which I included in the StoryMap and is what you see at the top of this post. The write-up I found left a lot to be desired, so I had to make a lot of alterations. If you want to know how I did it, contact me!

entry.title: Site Selection Retrospective
entry.summary: Back when I was a student at the University of Louisville in the Geography department, one of the most interesting projects I was…
entry.content:
Back when I was a student at the University of Louisville in the Geography department, one of the most interesting projects I was assigned was to perform a site suitability study.

A site suitability study is a straightforward concept, but in practice it can get complicated quickly. The idea is that given a certain set of criteria, geospatial analysis can find physical locations that best fit the conditions. There are two keys to good site selection.

The first is having a well-defined set of criteria. At a minimum these criteria should be categorized into desired traits vs required traits; ideally all conditions will be given a "weight" where some conditions are more important than others. 

The second key can be much harder to obtain (at least on the zero-dollar budget of a student!) and that is having quality supporting data. For a purely geographic study (e.g. finding the ideal location for a new campsite within a state park) the underlying data supporting the decision-making process is physical --- such as topography and hydrography --- and can usually be collected or obtained easily. In a commercial study, such as the case I used for my project, the kind of data needed is generally not the kind collected by public agencies --- such as locations of big box retailers and restaurants. Data that is collected by public agencies --- such as socio-economic factors and average daily traffic --- may only provided at a generalized level and may not always be the most representative. 

That being said, in my opinion having the well-defined criteria is the more important of the two keys. This opinion is backed up by my student project.

For my project I chose to search for the most suitable site for a new car wash in Louisville, specifically a Mike's Carwash. I spent my college years working at Mike's store number 45 and through that experience, I learned that the company had a very well-documented set of criteria they used when selecting a new site for an operation. 

I'll spare you the details of the entire process I used to calculate my final suitable site results, but essentially it involved dividing the city of Louisville into a grid of rectangles to serve as building blocks for suitable areas then calculating weighted values within each grid cell while taking into account the weighted values of nearby cells. All underlying data was obtained through publicly available means (who needs placer.ai) or physically mapped out by me to the best of my ability. Given the scope of this project (which was intended to be a proof of concept more than anything) I've always been pleased with how it turned out. 

Here are some of the findings:

The above map shows all Mike's Locations as of 2026

This map shows all the sites I identified as suitable for a new Mike's Location. Note that all Louisville Mike's locations and all sites identified by me are east of Interstate 65. Any native of Kentuckiana should not find that surprising given the criteria listed by the company.

This map of minimum bounding geometry helps illustrate the overlap better. The red polygon represents the area encompassed by all Mike's locations, the blue polygon represents the area encompassed by my suitable sites.

In the end, six car washes are located either completely within a suitable site or within 300 feet of a suitable site. Three of these are Mike's stores.

When I originally presented my project back in 2019, the single parcel that I determined to be most promising was home to a recently closed Payless shoe store. Everything about this site screamed potential for a car wash. If I wasn't a broke college student, I might have had a chance to make some money off my research because a few years later in 2022, someone saw the same opportunity as me and converted the site to an automatic car wash. Of course, I'm not privy to this company's financials, but based on the fact that I drive past this business every day as part of my commute to work --- it appears to be very successful.

This was my crude 3D rendering to enhance my pitch for the site.

This is what the site looked like when I was a student at U of L.

In this image taken from the new owner's website, it appears they have built a business charging $26 for an automatic car wash, I see a good-sized line there every day after I get off work.

It's nice to look back at something you did and know that you were on to something, even if it didn't result in any benefit to yourself. I'd really like to have an opportunity to do more of these kinds of studies in the future, not sure how that will play into a career in managing roadways for American Indian tribes... but who knows!

entry.title: Stand Out Proposals
entry.summary: As a consultant within a fast-growing department, I'm always looking for ways for my company to get our foot in the door with…
entry.content:
As a consultant within a fast-growing department, I'm always looking for ways for my company to get our foot in the door with a new client. Most of the high-revenue generating projects within my department can be attributed to roadway and bridge design projects as well as civil site development (not in my wheelhouse!). These projects bring in a lot of money but they can be the hardest to acquire.

American Indian Tribes are sovereign nations and as such are entitled to choose who they contract with to perform work. In fact, tribes are even exempt from Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, which prohibits discrimination in employment based on race or national origin. Essentially, tribal governments are allowed to apply "Indian Preference" when choosing a contractor. If a company is owned by Indians, they can receive varying degrees of preference in the contract awarding process --- as defined in each tribe's procurement standards.

Since roadway/bridge design projects and other engineering services are so expensive to tribes, they constitute a financial risk. One service that my company offers is Long Range Transportation Plan (LRTP) development. It's a cheap way for us to show off our work ethic, get to know the transportation staff personally and serve as a launchpad for other, more profitable ventures with the tribe. This is the primary focus of my work, and consequently I'm also the one putting together proposals for potential clients.

My employer has no enrolled Indians in our ownership body. How are we to compete with Indian-owned AEC firms? What can I, a mere geographer, do to increase our chances of being selected for a project? This is where the featured image of this post comes into play. 

Proposal requirements are usually pretty cut and dry, with not much room for creativity. While our team is seasoned and fully capable of delivering high-quality LRTPs, it's hard to convey that through walls of text detailing our prior experiences in this space. One thing I try to do when preparing a proposal is to make the cover page eye-catching and truly unique. I do this by making a custom map.

In this case, our potential client was the Standing Rock Sioux Tribe. Their reservation is bisected by the border between North and South Dakota, which I deliberately did not call attention to in this map. By leaving out this arbitrary imaginary line, created as a product of manifest destiny, our map communicates a subtle acknowledgement of their tribal sovereignty. 

One thing I also do whenever I am making a map for a client (whether it's for a proposal or not) is do some research on their history. One detail I discovered while researching this tribe is their special connection to the Missouri River, which forms the eastern boundary of their territory. Rather than having the red line territorial boundary run over the satellite imagery of the river, I instead chose to remove the eastern boundary line all together and insert a dark blue polygon of the river, which makes it stand out from the rest of the imagery. This decision is another subtle acknowledgement that the tribe's connection with the river is not just as a mere dividing line, but an integral part of the tribe's territory. 

I used some of my favorite font combinations on this map, which I discovered through trial and error. I always find that darkening the surrounding area and adding a subtle hillshade effect always produces a nice result.

Of course, a visually appealing map alone will not win any contracts, but it shows the reviewer before they even open the packet that we can make high-quality work that is tailored to the individual tribal client. 

We just submitted this proposal 2 days ago at the time of writing, I'll report back if we win the contract.

entry.title: Collecting Aerial Imagery
entry.summary: Flying a drone is scary. I do it all the time. When doing site visits, whether it is to meet with the client…
entry.content:
Flying a drone is scary. I do it all the time.

When doing site visits, whether it is to meet with the client or to perform field work, one thing that always travels with me is the department drone. We have access to a Skydio 2+, possibly the most fool-proof drone on the market. It's a far cry from the drones I learned to fly at the University of Louisville where the pilot was required to take corrective action to keep the thing stable at nearly all times. Thank goodness I learned what I did then and got my FAA Part 107 Certification before I got too lazy on the Skydio! The Skydio 2+ takes off and lands nearly autonomously, has object detection that prevents the drone from colliding with tree branches and telephone wire, and has nearly lossless video streaming back to the controller. It's a real treat to fly.

Well, it would be, if it weren't for everything else. 

Unfortunately for me, the conditions I am required to fly our Skydio are often not ideal. Usually I am taking profile photos of bridges over creeks, rivers and bayous. Even with collision avoidance technology, getting a drone far enough away from a bridge to get a good shot is like threading a needle. Tree branches love to stretch out over narrow bodies of water from both banks, creating a kind of webbed matrix of woody sinew. Get too close to a branch and the drone will violently recoil in the air--- so hard that it might push itself dangerously close to a branch reaching from the other side of the water body, triggering a dangerous snowball effect of violent thrashing from the drone as it attempts to remove itself from the situation. 

Another hazard of flying low to the ground over undeveloped terrain is avian threats. Yes, you read that correctly. I can't tell you how many close calls I've had resulting from near suicidal barrages of small birds attempting to attack our drone. Fortunately I have not injured one of these brave warriors yet, but it is always something to be vigilant for. 

Finally, takeoff and landing can make your blood pressure spike in certain conditions. There are often times where the bridge I need to snap a photo of are part of a major arterial road or even an interstate. These kinds of roads usually don't leave much room in the right-of-way for cars to pull over, much less to take off and land a drone. Many times, this procedure has to be a carefully coordinated affair. One thing you never want to do is take off a drone where drivers can see it, lest they get distracted and cause a collision. When a gap in traffic presents itself, the drone needs to be launched from the roadside quickly and gain as much altitude as possible before another vehicle comes along to potentially see it. The drone must traverse the narrow right-of-way clearing between roadway and tree line, careful to account for the massive wind gusts created by tractor trailers barreling down the road. These tractor trailers also cause an instinctual fear response when they barrel past the pilot (me!) at highway speeds--- it's something that I have to consciously suppress. 

In the end though, the cool-factor of flying drones as part of your work outweighs the stress induced by the operation of said drones. Sometimes you get to capture interesting spots that may be used by engineers to develop on. The picture featured in this post is being used to help develop a revenue-generating site for the Coushatta Tribe in Louisiana. Eventually there will be a roundabout here that facilitates easy in-and-out access to a travel center, which should be a great boon to the tribe. Further north in the state, near the Jena Band of Choctaw Indians headquarters, I snapped the cover photo for this website. Depicting a bridge on US84 over Little River.

entry.title: Ramah Navajo Wall Map
entry.summary: One of the perplexing things about moving up in the field of geography is that the higher you climb the career ladder, the…
entry.content:
One of the perplexing things about moving up in the field of geography is that the higher you climb the career ladder, the fewer maps you are asked to make. While having more experience designing maps generally leads to the ability to create higher-quality products, when more responsibilities are given to a geographer, often the first category of task that is pushed down to lower-level employees is cartography.

This is why I was thrilled when the Ramah Navajo Department of Transportation specifically requested me to make a poster-sized map of their National Tribal Transportation Facility Inventory; which I had spent the last few months preparing for them. 

When producing this map, I looked to the seal of the Ramah Navajo for palette inspiration, which is what led to the choice of colors used in the boundaries of the reservation, legend box and routes themselves. 

I also generally shy away from using pure black text whenever possible. I find that it is too harsh on the eyes and I always try and opt for some other dark variant. In this case, I took a representative color sample from the aerial imagery and turned down the HSV values until I had a rich dark brown that was clearly legible but still felt at home in the desert landscape captured in the imagery. 

The client loved the map and told me they must guard it from others in their office who want to take it for themselves. I told her I'm always happy to make more.

entry.title: American Indian Lands in the Contiguous United States
entry.summary: The geography of Indian Country in the U.S. is in constant flux. As tribes gain federal recognition, land is transferred from fee simple…
entry.content:
The geography of Indian Country in the U.S. is in constant flux. As tribes gain federal recognition, land is transferred from fee simple title to trust, and judicial decisions re-establish sovereignty... any map of American Indian land practically becomes outdated the moment it is produced. This map is a passion project that aims to capture the state of American Indian land in the lower 48 states as of April 2025. This map was presented at the 2026 National Tribal GIS Conference in Albuquerque, New Mexico

For a higher-resolution version of this map, contact me!
